readerTitle: Your hourly rate is the floor, not the price
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 운영 컨설턴트, 구독형 소프트웨어 회사의 UX 컨설턴트) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 컨설팅 가격은 내 비용으로 바닥을, 고객이 얻는 가치로 천장을 정하고 그 사이에서 고른다.
misconception: 컨설팅은 시간 단가 × 예상 시간으로 청구하는 것이 가장 공정하고 정확하다.

sources.text: 가격 전략의 표준 개념 (원가 기반 가격, 가치 기반 가격)

factChecks.note: 원가 바닥: ($60,000 + $12,000) ÷ 800시간 = 시간당 $90. 20시간 프로젝트 = $1,800. 연 800 청구 시간은 영업·행정 시간을 뺀 가정치입니다.
소프트웨어: 원가 바닥 $110 × 30시간 = $3,300. 월 체험 2,000명, 전환율 10% → 11%이면 월 20명 추가 × 고객 생애 가치 $600 = 월 $12,000, 연 $144,000. 견적 $15,000은 상승분 약 1.25개월치입니다.

cards.title: Your hourly rate is the floor, not the price
body: Maya ran kitchens for 12 years. Now she consults. A restaurant owner asks her to cut the food he throws away.
She thinks it will take 20 hours. Her first instinct is to multiply hours by a rate. That number turns out to be the least interesting one on the table.

image.label: A consultant with a clipboard beside a kitchen waste bin
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 레스토랑 주방 뒤편에서 컨설턴트가 클립보드를 들고 음식물 쓰레기통을 살펴보고, 옆에서 셰프 복장의 사장이 팔짱을 끼고 지켜봄. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should Maya price the project?
body: She needs about $90 an hour to cover her costs and pay herself. The restaurant buys $30,000 of food a month and throws out about 10% of it. Maya has cut waste by a third in similar kitchens.

options.feedback: This is **cost-plus pricing**: safe, because it covers her costs. But it ignores what the owner gains, so she leaves most of the value on the table.

options.text: A fixed fee of $4,500, explained against the expected savings
options.feedback: This is **value-based pricing** with cost as the floor. She earns well above her $1,800 minimum, and the owner still keeps most of the gain.

options.text: Half of whatever the restaurant saves over the next year
options.feedback: It ties her pay to value, but savings are hard to measure and easy to dispute. She could wait a year and argue over the total.

cards.title: Where $90 an hour comes from.
body: Most consultants can't bill 2,000 hours a year. Finding clients, admin and travel eat much of the week. Maya assumes 800 billable hours.
So 20 hours means a **$1,800 floor**. Below that, she is paying to work.

breakdown.label: Pay for herself
breakdown.detail: What she wants to earn in a year

breakdown.label: Hourly floor
breakdown.detail: Cost-plus: the minimum, not the target

cards.title: Now look from the owner's side.
body: The restaurant throws out about $3,000 of food a month. Cutting that by a third saves $1,000 a month, or **$12,000 a year**.
At $1,800, Maya would charge 15% of the first year's savings. At $4,500, it's about 38%. The owner still keeps $7,500 in year one, and more after that.
Cost tells her the lowest price she can accept. Value tells her the highest price the owner could sensibly pay. Her price belongs between the two.

image.label: A price range from $1,800 floor to $12,000 ceiling
image.brief: 가로 눈금자 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 끝 "Cost floor $1,800", 오른쪽 끝 "Value to client $12,000", 중간에 강조된 핀 "Maya's fee $4,500". 핀 오른쪽 구간에 "Client keeps $7,500" 라벨.

cards.title: "So what's your hourly rate?"
body: The owner likes the plan but frowns at $4,500. He asks for her hourly rate. How should Maya answer?

options.feedback: It pulls the talk back to cost-plus. Now he will count her hours instead of his savings, and either side can feel cheated.

options.text: "It's a fixed fee for the result. The project targets about $12,000 a year in savings."
options.feedback: This keeps the frame on value-based pricing. He compares $4,500 with what he gains, not with a wage.
Still above her $1,800 floor, so she doesn't lose money. But a quick drop tells him the price was never tied to anything.

cards.title: Value only counts if the client believes it.
body: Maya's $12,000 is an estimate. To the owner, it's a promise. If he doubts it, a value-based fee feels like a gamble.
Make the value concrete. Show results from similar kitchens, or start with a smaller paid review that measures his actual waste first.
And remember the floor. A client who only values the work at $1,000 isn't a bargain. They're a loss.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: A subscription software company asks a design consultant to fix its sign-up flow. Her floor is $110 an hour for 30 hours: $3,300.

About 2,000 people start a free trial each month, and 10% become paying users. Each paying user is worth about $600 over time. Lifting conversion to 11% adds about $12,000 of value every month. What should she quote?

options.feedback: Cost-plus covers her costs but prices the job like a wage. The client gets about a week's worth of gains back for a whole year of benefit.

options.text: $15,000 fixed, with a clear scope and a results check after launch
options.feedback: Value-based and believable: about five weeks of the expected gain, well above her floor. The results check makes the value easier to trust.

options.text: $60,000, since a year of gains is worth $144,000
options.feedback: Still under the ceiling, but a one-point lift is a guess. The more of the value she claims, the more certain the client needs to feel.

cards.callout: Same logic as the kitchen: cost sets the floor, value sets the room above it.

cards.title: Price the result, and use your costs as the floor.
body: You used two ideas. **Cost-plus pricing** gave the minimum you can accept. **Value-based pricing** showed how much room sits above it, and how to explain the fee.
**Try it today:** take one service you sell. Write your cost floor, then estimate what the result is worth to the customer. Where does your current price sit between them?
